wa_centralwest.blurb: This is the western Cascades climbing zone that stretches east of Seattle: the Skykomish Valley around Index, the I-90 corridor near North Bend, the Snoqualmie Pass area and the Western Alpine Lakes. Most crags sit within an hour or so of the city. Bouldering, sport and trad come in roughly equal shares, with a little alpine, ice and mixed on top. Bolted lines mostly fall between 5.10 and 5.12, with a decent supply of moderates, and the boulder problems cover the full range from easy to very hard. The valley walls near Index are granite, and the trad there has a reputation for being stiff for its grade. Around North Bend you find steep, well-bolted sport crags from beginner level up to the top end. Higher areas keep snow later, so the main season runs from late spring through autumn, while the lower crags often work from April to December if the rain holds off.

co_grand_junction_area.blurb: Grand Junction sits on Colorado's western slope and serves as a base for several very different desert and canyon venues, among them Unaweep Canyon, Colorado National Monument, Escalante Canyon and the Grand Mesa. Most of the climbing here is bouldering, with a solid share of trad and a smaller amount of sport. Roped routes are mostly 5.8 to 5.11, with a thinner tail of harder climbs, and the boulders run mainly from V0 to V5. Unaweep holds granite and gneiss cliffs from short crags to walls of several hundred feet, with crack, sport and multipitch lines, and some sandstone bouldering. The Monument and Escalante offer sandstone towers and cracks. Spring and autumn are the most comfortable seasons, though a sun or shade choice keeps climbing possible through much of the year. It tends to be less crowded than Moab.

ut_central_wasatch.blurb: The Central Wasatch is the cluster of canyons in the mountains directly east of Salt Lake City, with Little Cottonwood and Big Cottonwood by far the largest. Little Cottonwood is mostly granitic rock, with concentrated walls and a huge amount of bouldering. Big Cottonwood is mainly quartzite, with roadside multipitch trad and single-pitch bolted lines. Smaller venues include Ferguson, Mount Olympus and Lone Peak Cirque. Trad is the biggest discipline, followed by bouldering and sport, with some alpine and ice. Roped climbs are mostly 5.8 to 5.12, and the boulders stretch from easy up to very hard. Fall and spring are the sweet spot; south-facing slabs work in winter and shaded or higher walls suit summer. The canyons are a short drive from the city, so there is a strong local scene.

ut_southeast_utah.blurb: Southeast Utah covers the red-rock desert around Moab and further south, with Indian Creek, Potash Road, River Road, Castle Valley, Fisher Towers and the La Sal Mountains among its biggest areas. Trad dominates, mostly crack climbing, with a smaller number of sport routes and boulder problems and a handful of aid lines. Most roped climbs fall between 5.9 and 5.12, with many in the 5.10 to 5.11 range. The rock is sandstone in several layers: Wingate gives clean splitter cracks, Navajo is solid along the road cliffs, Entrada is soft and Cutler is crumbly. Spring and autumn are the pleasant seasons, since summer heat and winter frost both bite. Bring plenty of cams, and avoid the rock when it is wet because the sandstone weakens.

ky_red_river_gorge.blurb: The Red River Gorge is a forested canyon system in east-central Kentucky, near the town of Slade, set in a rolling plateau cut by streams into sandstone cliff lines, rock shelters and natural arches. The climbing is on sandstone, mostly steep and overhanging, with pockets, ledges and weathered holes in place of crimps. Cliffs are mostly under 200 feet, so routes are largely single-pitch. Sport dominates, with a good number of trad lines and a modest amount of bouldering. Most routes fall between 5.10 and 5.13, with plenty of moderates below that and a handful at the top end. The area is spread out across many separate crags, including the Northern Gorge, Muir Valley and several recreational preserves.

ca_bishop_area.blurb: Bishop lies in the Owens Valley on the east side of the Sierra, and offers three distinct kinds of climbing close to town. Bouldering is the biggest draw, spread over the Buttermilk Country, the Volcanic Tablelands and smaller zones; the problems range from easy to very hard, and many are tall. Sport is nearly as big, led by the Owens River Gorge, a long canyon of bolted routes mostly from the 5.10s to 5.12. Pine Creek Canyon adds granite cracks and bolted lines, and is the usual summer choice. The gorge and the boulders are best in the cooler months from late fall through spring. Trad is a smaller share and the alpine objectives sit higher up.
